title: Korean grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Korean, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is natural Seoul Korean in the polite style people use with anyone they don't know well, written in Hangul with a reading in Latin letters (Revised Romanization).

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Korean conversation.
lessons.topic: {{저는|jeoneun}} … {{이에요|ieyo}} / {{예요|yeyo}} “I am …”, and the final consonant that decides which

dialog.tr: Hello! I'm Kim Minjun.
Hello. I'm Emily.
Emily, are you American?
Yes, I'm American. And you, Minjun?
I'm Korean. Nice to meet you!
Nice to meet you!

blocks.p: Look at the end of each sentence: {{이에요|ieyo}} or {{예요|yeyo}}. That is Korean's “am, is, are”, and it goes **after** the word, at the very end. {{저는 에밀리예요|jeoneun emilliyeyo}} is, word for word, “as for me, Emily-am”. In Korean, the word that does the saying always comes last.

{{저는|jeoneun}} is “I” at the start of a sentence: {{저|jeo}} “I” (the polite word) and {{는|neun}}, a little ending that means “as for”. {{네|ne}} is “yes”, {{아니요|aniyo}} is “no”, and {{안녕하세요|annyeonghaseyo}} is “hello” at any time of day.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a place or a thing: Emily, Korea, coffee, student.

the consonant at the bottom of a Korean syllable block, like {{ㄴ}} in {{한|han}} or {{ㅁ}} in {{람|ram}}. Koreans call it {{받침|batchim}}. Many endings have one shape after a final consonant and another after a vowel.

blocks.p: **이에요 or 예요?** It depends on how the noun before it ends. After a final consonant, {{이에요|ieyo}}; after a vowel, {{예요|yeyo}}. This kind of choice comes back with almost every ending in Korean, so it's worth getting used to now.

**No “you”.** Korean has a word for “you”, {{당신|dangsin}}, but it sounds rude or romantic, so you don't say it to someone you've just met. Use the person's name with {{씨|ssi}} (like “Mr.” or “Ms.”, but after the first name), or simply leave “you” out: {{미국 사람이에요?|miguk saramieyo?}} on its own already means “Are you American?”. Never put {{씨|ssi}} after your own name.

**Questions** are the same sentence with your voice going up at the end: {{학생이에요.|haksaengieyo.}} “I'm a student.”, {{학생이에요?|haksaengieyo?}} “Are you a student?”. And {{…씨는요?|…ssineunyo?}} turns the question back: “and you?”.

ex.note: said to Sujin herself: her name instead of “you”

blocks.tip: **Reading Hangul.** Korean letters are grouped into syllable blocks: {{한|han}} is {{ㅎ}} h + {{ㅏ}} a + {{ㄴ}} n, “han”. There are only 24 letters, and most learners can read them after a few hours. Until then, the reading in Latin letters tells you how to say each example, and tapping an example lets you hear it.

mistakes.why: {{학생|haksaeng}} ends in a consonant ({{ㅇ}}), so it takes {{이에요|ieyo}}.
{{당신|dangsin}} sounds rude to someone you've just met. Leave “you” out, or use their name with {{씨|ssi}}.
{{씨|ssi}} is for other people's names, never your own.

lessons.title: Point at things and ask what they are
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?”, name things, and say “no, it isn't”.
lessons.topic: {{이거|igeo}}, {{그거|geugeo}}, {{저거|jeogeo}} “this, that”; {{뭐예요?|mwoyeyo?}} “what is it?”; {{아니에요|anieyo}} “it isn't”

dialog.tr: Excuse me, what's this?
That? It's rice cake.
And what's that over there? Is it gimbap?
No, it isn't gimbap. It's sundae, Korean sausage.
Oh, really?

blocks.p: **Three ways to point.** Korean has three pointing words, by distance: {{이|i}} “this” (near me), {{그|geu}} “that” (near you, or something we just mentioned) and {{저|jeo}} “that over there” (far from us both). Before a noun they work like “this” and “that” in English. On their own, add {{거|geo}} “thing”: {{이거|igeo}} “this (thing)”.

**Asking.** {{뭐예요?|mwoyeyo?}} is “what is it?”: {{뭐|mwo}} “what” and {{예요|yeyo}} (it ends in a vowel). The question word sits where the answer will go: {{이거 뭐예요?|igeo mwoyeyo?}} “this what-is?”, {{이거 떡이에요.|igeo tteogieyo.}} “this rice-cake-is”.

**It isn't.** To say what something isn't, use {{아니에요|anieyo}} “isn't”, with {{이|i}} or {{가|ga}} on the noun before it: {{김밥이 아니에요|gimbabi anieyo}} “it isn't gimbap”. {{이|i}} after a consonant, {{가|ga}} after a vowel. (You'll meet this {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}} again in lesson 4.)

ex.note: the phone is near the person you're talking to

ex.tr: That over there is my house.
ex.note: {{우리 집|uri jip}} “our house”: Koreans say “our” for their home and family

blocks.tip: **Reading the readings.** **eo** ({{ㅓ}}) is like the “u” in “cup”, said a little deeper; **eu** ({{ㅡ}}) is like the “oo” in “good” with the lips spread; **ae** and **e** ({{ㅐ}}, {{ㅔ}}) both sound like the “e” in “bed”. At the start of a word, **g, d, b, j** are soft, halfway to **k, t, p, ch**.

{{커피|keopi}} ends in a vowel: {{가|ga}}.

lessons.title: Ask for things in a café or a shop
lessons.summary: Order a drink, ask for water or the menu, and answer the staff's questions: “One americano, please.”
lessons.topic: {{주세요|juseyo}} “please give me”; {{좀|jom}} to soften; {{여기요|yeogiyo}} / {{저기요|jeogiyo}}; short answers with {{요|yo}}

dialog.tr: Welcome. What can I get you?
One iced americano, please.
What size?
A large one, please.
Sure. For here?
No, to go.

blocks.p: **One word does it all.** {{주세요|juseyo}} means “please give me”. Say what you want, then {{주세요|juseyo}}: {{물 주세요|mul juseyo}} “Water, please.” It's polite enough for any café, shop or restaurant, and it comes last, like every verb in Korean.

**One, or this one.** Add {{하나|hana}} “one” **after** the thing: {{아메리카노 하나 주세요|amerikano hana juseyo}}, word for word “americano one please-give”. (Counting more comes in lesson 13.) Pointing works too: {{이거 주세요|igeo juseyo}} “This one, please.”

**Softer, and calling the staff.** {{좀|jom}} “a little” just before {{주세요|juseyo}} makes a request softer, like “could I have”: {{물 좀 주세요|mul jom juseyo}} “Could I have some water?”. To call a waiter, say {{여기요!|yeogiyo!}} or {{저기요!|jeogiyo!}} (“here!”, “excuse me!”): in Korea, that's normal and polite.

**Short answers.** When someone asks you something, you can answer with just the word and {{요|yo}}, which keeps it polite: {{테이크아웃이요.|teikeuausiyo.}} “To go.”, {{하나요.|hanayo.}} “One.” After a consonant it's {{이요|iyo}}, after a vowel {{요|yo}}.

ex.tr: Could I see the menu, please?
Excuse me! Could we have some more kimchi?
ex.note: {{더|deo}} “more”: side dishes are refilled for free in Korean restaurants

blocks.tip: {{뭐 드릴까요?|mwo deurilkkayo?}} “What can I get you?” is what staff say; you don't need to make that form yet, just recognise it. {{감사합니다|gamsahamnida}} “thank you” finishes any order nicely.

lessons.title: Say what you have and what there is
lessons.summary: Ask whether there's Wi-Fi, say you have a question, or that there's no milk: one pair of words does it all.
lessons.topic: {{있어요|isseoyo}} / {{없어요|eopseoyo}} “there is, have / there isn't, don't have”; the subject particle {{이|i}} / {{가|ga}}

dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there Wi-Fi here?
Yes, there is. The password is this.
Thank you. And there's no towel.
Oh, I'm sorry. Here you are.

blocks.p: **Two words, many jobs.** {{있어요|isseoyo}} means “there is”, “I have” and “it's there”; {{없어요|eopseoyo}} is the opposite: “there isn't”, “I don't have”. English needs different words; Korean doesn't. {{시간이 있어요|sigani isseoyo}} is both “there is time” and “I have time”.

blocks.means: a short ending stuck to a word to show what job it does in the sentence, like {{는|neun}} in {{저는|jeoneun}}. Korean has about a dozen everyday ones, and you'll learn them one at a time.
who or what a sentence is about: the one doing something, or the one that is (or is there). In {{차가 있어요|chaga isseoyo}} “I have a car”, it's the car.

blocks.p: **The subject particle {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}}.** The thing that is there, or that you have, gets {{이|i}} after a consonant and {{가|ga}} after a vowel. Korean sees “I have a car” as “a car exists (for me)”, so the car is the subject: {{차가 있어요|chaga isseoyo}}.

table: {{차가 있어요|chaga isseoyo}} I have a car
{{돈이 없어요|doni eopseoyo}} I have no money

blocks.p: **Who has it?** Say who first, with {{저는|jeoneun}}: {{저는 고양이가 있어요|jeoneun goyangiga isseoyo}} “I have a cat” (as for me, a cat exists). In everyday speech, Koreans often drop the particle: {{시간 있어요?|sigan isseoyo?}} is how most people actually ask “Do you have time?”. Learn it with the particle; dropping it comes naturally later.

ex.tr: I have a younger brother or sister.
ex.note: {{동생|dongsaeng}} is a younger sibling of either sex

blocks.tip: {{있어요?|isseoyo?}} with your voice going up is the easiest question in Korean: in a shop, {{봉투 있어요?|bongtu isseoyo?}} “Do you have a bag?”; to a friend, {{시간 있어요?|sigan isseoyo?}} “Are you free?”.

mistakes.why: {{시간|sigan}} ends in a consonant: {{이|i}}.
{{아니에요|anieyo}} is “it isn't (something)”: {{저는 차가 아니에요|jeoneun chaga anieyo}} means “I am not a car”! Not having is {{없어요|eopseoyo}}.

lessons.title: Ask and say where things are
lessons.summary: Ask where the restroom or the station is, and say where things are: on the desk, next to the bank, in your bag.
lessons.topic: {{어디에 있어요?|eodie isseoyo?}} “where is it?”; a place + {{에|e}} “at, in”; {{위|wi}}, {{아래|arae}}, {{앞|ap}}, {{뒤|dwi}}, {{옆|yeop}}, {{안|an}}

dialog.tr: Excuse me, where's the restroom?
The restroom? It's over there, next to the elevator.
Thank you. And where's the convenience store?
The convenience store is on the first floor.
Oh, thank you!

blocks.p: **Where is it?** {{어디|eodi}} is “where”, and {{에|e}} after a place means “at” or “in”. So {{어디에 있어요?|eodie isseoyo?}} is “where-at is-it?”, and the answer puts the place where {{어디|eodi}} was: {{일 층에 있어요|il cheunge isseoyo}} “it's on the first floor”. In speech, {{어디 있어요?|eodi isseoyo?}} without {{에|e}} is common too.
**On, under, next to.** Korean says “the desk's top”, not “on the desk”: first the thing, then a place word, then {{에|e}}. {{책상 위에|chaeksang wie}} is “on the desk” (desk top-at).

table: {{은행 앞에|eunhaeng ape}} in front of the bank
{{편의점 옆에|pyeonuijeom yeope}} next to the convenience store

blocks.p: **Here and there.** {{여기|yeogi}} “here”, {{거기|geogi}} “there (near you)”, {{저기|jeogi}} “over there”: the same {{이|i}}, {{그|geu}}, {{저|jeo}} as in lesson 2. In speech they're used without {{에|e}}: {{여기 있어요|yeogi isseoyo}} “it's here”.

blocks.means: what a sentence is about: “as for…”. Korean marks it with {{은|eun}} (after a consonant) or {{는|neun}} (after a vowel). In {{저는 학생이에요|jeoneun haksaengieyo}}, the topic is “I”.

blocks.p: **Asking about something new.** In {{편의점은 어디에 있어요?|pyeonuijeomeun eodie isseoyo?}} the store gets {{은|eun}}, as {{저|jeo}} did in {{저는|jeoneun}}: “and as for the convenience store, where is it?”. When you turn to something new, {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}} is the natural choice. For your first question, {{화장실이|hwajangsiri}} with {{이|i}} works just as well; lesson 10 shows the difference.

ex.tr: The phone is in the bag.
The bank is next to the post office.
The cat is under the bed.
My friend is in Seoul now.

blocks.tip: {{어디예요?|eodiyeyo?}} “where is it?” is a short way to ask about a place: {{화장실이 어디예요?|hwajangsiri eodiyeyo?}}. It's as polite as {{어디에 있어요?|eodie isseoyo?}}.

mistakes.why: The thing first, then the place word: “desk top-at”, not “on desk”.

mistakes.tr: The bank is next to the post office.
mistakes.why: Where something is takes {{에|e}}: {{옆에|yeope}} “next to”.

lessons.title: Say what you want to do
lessons.summary: Say what you'd like to do, and ask others what they want to do: “I want to learn Korean.”
lessons.topic: verbs and their stem; the object particle {{을|eul}} / {{를|reul}}; stem + {{-고 싶어요|-go sipeoyo}} “want to”

dialog.tr: What do you want to do in Korea?
I want to eat Korean food.

dialog.t: 아, 그래요? 또 뭐 하고 싶어요?
dialog.tr: Oh, really? What else do you want to do?
dialog.r: a, geuraeyo? tto mwo hago sipeoyo?

dialog.tr: I want to meet Korean friends.
Great!

blocks.means: a word for doing or being: eat, go, learn, have. In Korean it comes at the end of the sentence.

blocks.p: **The dictionary form.** Every Korean verb has a dictionary form ending in {{다|da}}: {{먹다|meokda}} “to eat”, {{가다|gada}} “to go”, {{배우다|baeuda}} “to learn”. Take off {{다|da}} and you have the **stem**, the part every ending is added to: {{먹|meok}}, {{가|ga}}, {{배우|baeu}}.

blocks.means: the part of a verb that stays the same: the dictionary form without {{다|da}}. {{먹다|meokda}} → {{먹|meok}}.

blocks.p: **Want to.** Add {{-고 싶어요|-go sipeoyo}} to the stem: {{먹고 싶어요|meokgo sipeoyo}} “I want to eat”, {{가고 싶어요|gago sipeoyo}} “I want to go”. It never changes shape, whatever the stem ends in. Ask with your voice going up: {{뭐 하고 싶어요?|mwo hago sipeoyo?}} “What do you want to do?” ({{하다|hada}} “to do” → {{하고 싶어요|hago sipeoyo}}).

blocks.means: the person or thing an action is done to: in “I eat bread”, the bread. Korean marks it with the particle {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}.

blocks.p: **The object particle {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}.** The thing you eat, learn or watch gets {{을|eul}} after a consonant and {{를|reul}} after a vowel: {{비빔밥을 먹고 싶어요|bibimbabeul meokgo sipeoyo}}, {{한국어를 배우고 싶어요|hangugeoreul baeugo sipeoyo}}. The order is: who, what, and the verb last. English says “I want to eat bibimbap”; Korean says “I bibimbap eat-want”.

ex.tr: I want to watch a movie.
What do you want to eat?
I want to rest a little.

ex.note: word for word “I want to see”: what Koreans say to someone they miss

blocks.tip: {{-고 싶어요|-go sipeoyo}} is about what **you** want, or what you ask someone else (“do you want to?”). For a third person, Koreans add more: that comes much later. For now: “I want to…” and “Do you want to…?”.

mistakes.why: The verb, with its ending, goes last.
{{커피|keopi}} ends in a vowel: {{를|reul}}.
Endings go on the stem: take off {{다|da}} first.

practice.tr: I want to watch a movie.
practice.why: The movie is the object, and {{영화|yeonghwa}} ends in a vowel: {{를|reul}}.

lessons.title: Say what you do every day
lessons.summary: Talk about your day: what you eat, drink, watch and do. Your first real verb ending.
lessons.topic: the present tense {{-아요|-ayo}} / {{-어요|-eoyo}} / {{해요|haeyo}}, chosen by the stem's last vowel

dialog.tr: What do you eat in the morning, Sophie?

dialog.t: 저는 빵을 먹어요. 그리고 커피를 마셔요.
dialog.tr: I eat bread. And I drink coffee.
dialog.r: jeoneun ppangeul meogeoyo. geurigo keopireul masyeoyo.

dialog.tr: I eat rice.
Oh, really? And what do you do in the evening?
In the evening I work out. And I watch dramas.

blocks.p: **The polite present.** In lesson 6 you added {{-고 싶어요|-go sipeoyo}} to a stem. Now the main ending: the present tense, for what you do in general or right now. It has three shapes, and the stem's **last vowel** chooses.

blocks.means: the form of a verb that says when something happens: the present (I eat), the past (I ate), the future (I will eat).
choosing an ending by the vowel before it. In Korean, a stem whose last vowel is {{ㅏ}} or {{ㅗ}} takes {{-아|-a}}; any other vowel takes {{-어|-eo}}.

blocks.p: **Shortened forms.** When the stem ends in a vowel, the two vowels melt together, and the short form is the only one people say: {{ㅏ}} + {{아|a}} stays {{ㅏ}}, {{ㅗ}} + {{아|a}} becomes {{ㅘ}}, {{ㅣ}} + {{어|eo}} becomes {{ㅕ}}, {{ㅜ}} + {{어|eo}} becomes {{ㅝ}}.

**One form, many meanings.** {{먹어요|meogeoyo}} is “I eat”, “you eat”, “she eats”, and with your voice going up, “do you eat?”. Who it is comes from the sentence or the situation: Koreans leave out “I” and “you” whenever it's clear. The order is who, when, what, and the verb last: {{저는 매일 커피를 마셔요|jeoneun maeil keopireul masyeoyo}} “I every-day coffee drink”.

ex.tr: I meet my friends at the weekend.
My younger sibling reads a lot of books.
What are you doing? / What do you do?
I watch dramas in the evening.

blocks.tip: Many verbs are a noun + {{하다|hada}}: {{공부|gongbu}} “study” → {{공부하다|gongbuhada}} “to study”, {{운동|undong}} “exercise” → {{운동하다|undonghada}} “to work out”, {{요리|yori}} “cooking” → {{요리하다|yorihada}} “to cook”. They all end in {{해요|haeyo}}: one form for hundreds of verbs.

mistakes.why: {{마시|masi}} + {{어요|eoyo}} melts into {{마셔요|masyeoyo}}: nobody says the long form.
The vowel of {{먹|meok}} is {{ㅓ}}, not {{ㅏ}} or {{ㅗ}}: {{-어요|-eoyo}}.
{{하다|hada}} always becomes {{해요|haeyo}}.

lessons.title: Say where you go and where you do things
lessons.summary: Say where you're going and where things happen: “I'm going to the gym. I work out at the gym.”
lessons.topic: {{에|e}} “to” (going) and “at, in” (being somewhere); {{에서|eseo}} “at, in” (doing something)

goal.tr: I'm going to the library. I study at the library.

blocks.p: **Two particles for places.** Korean asks a question English doesn't: is someone just going somewhere or being there, or is something being **done** there?

table: {{학교에 가요|hakgyoe gayo}} I go to school
{{학교에서 공부해요|hakgyoeseo gongbuhaeyo}} I study at school

blocks.p: **The test is the verb.** With {{가요|gayo}} “go”, {{와요|wayo}} “come”, {{있어요|isseoyo}} and {{없어요|eopseoyo}}, the place takes {{에|e}}. With an action ({{먹어요|meogeoyo}}, {{공부해요|gongbuhaeyo}}, {{일해요|ilhaeyo}}, {{만나요|mannayo}}…), the place where it happens takes {{에서|eseo}}. Each has one shape, after a consonant or a vowel.

**{{에서|eseo}} also means “from”.** {{어디에서 왔어요?|eodieseo wasseoyo?}} “Where are you from?” (word for word “where-from came?”) is how Koreans ask where you're from. The answer: {{미국에서 왔어요|migugeseo wasseoyo}} “I'm from America.” ({{왔어요|wasseoyo}} “came” is a past form: lesson 17.)

ex.tr: A friend is coming to my place.
I have lunch at a restaurant.
I go for a walk in the park.

ex.note: word for word “I came from the UK”

blocks.tip: {{어디 가요?|eodi gayo?}} “Where are you going?” is also a friendly greeting between neighbors and coworkers, like “Off somewhere?”. A short answer is enough: {{회사에 가요.|hoesae gayo.}}

lessons.title: Say what you don't do
lessons.summary: Say no to things (“I don't eat meat”, “I don't drink”) and say what you only have.
lessons.topic: {{안|an}} + verb; {{-지 않아요|-ji anayo}}; {{만|man}} “only”

dialog.tr: What can I get you?

dialog.t: 저는 고기를 안 먹어요. 비빔밥에 고기가 있어요?
dialog.tr: I don't eat meat. Is there meat in the bibimbap?
dialog.r: jeoneun gogireul an meogeoyo. bibimbabe gogiga isseoyo?

dialog.t: 네, 감사합니다. 그리고 저는 술을 안 마셔요. 물만 주세요.
dialog.tr: Yes, thank you. And I don't drink alcohol. Just water, please.

blocks.p: **Put {{안|an}} before the verb.** {{먹어요|meogeoyo}} “I eat” → {{안 먹어요|an meogeoyo}} “I don't eat”. That's all: the verb keeps its ending, and {{안|an}} comes right before it.

**Noun + {{하다|hada}} verbs** put {{안|an}} between the two parts: {{공부해요|gongbuhaeyo}} → {{공부 안 해요|gongbu an haeyo}} “I don't study”, {{운동해요|undonghaeyo}} → {{운동 안 해요|undong an haeyo}} “I don't work out”.

**The longer way: {{-지 않아요|-ji anayo}}.** Stem + {{-지 않아요|-ji anayo}} means the same: {{먹지 않아요|meokji anayo}} “I don't eat”. It sounds a little more careful and is common in writing; in conversation {{안|an}} is more usual. Both are polite.

**Only: {{만|man}}.** {{만|man}} after a noun means “only, just”: {{물만 주세요|mulman juseyo}} “Just water, please.” With an object, it takes the place of {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}: {{채소만 먹어요|chaesoman meogeoyo}} “I only eat vegetables.”

ex.tr: I'm not going to work today.
My younger sibling doesn't work out.
Meat, I don't eat. Fish, I do.

blocks.tip: Look at the last example: {{고기는|gogineun}}, {{생선은|saengseoneun}}. When you contrast two things (this, but not that), Koreans mark them with {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}} instead of {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}. Lesson 10 shows more of this.

mistakes.why: With a noun + {{하다|hada}} verb, {{안|an}} goes just before {{해요|haeyo}}.
{{안|an}} comes right before the verb, never after it.
{{만|man}} takes the place of {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}.

lessons.title: Say what you like, and what others like
lessons.summary: Say what you like and don't like, say “me too!”, and compare yourself with someone else.
lessons.topic: {{좋아해요|joahaeyo}} (with {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}) and {{좋아요|joayo}} (with {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}}); {{싫어해요|sireohaeyo}}; {{도|do}} “too”; {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}} for contrast

dialog.tr: Sarah, do you like Korean food?
Yes, I do! I really like kimchi stew.
I like kimchi stew too. What about samgyetang?
Samgyetang, I don't really like.

dialog.t: 아, 그래요? 저는 삼계탕이 정말 좋아요!
dialog.tr: Oh, really? I love samgyetang!
dialog.r: a, geuraeyo? jeoneun samgyetangi jeongmal joayo!

blocks.p: **Two ways to say “like”.** {{좋아해요|joahaeyo}} (from {{좋아하다|joahada}}) is “like” as an action: what you like is its object, with {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}: {{김치를 좋아해요|gimchireul joahaeyo}}. {{좋아요|joayo}} (from {{좋다|jota}} “to be good”) is “it's good (to me)”: the thing is its subject, with {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}}: {{김치가 좋아요|gimchiga joayo}}. Both mean “I like kimchi”. {{좋아해요|joahaeyo}} is the safe one, and the only one for talking about other people.

table: {{싫어요|sireoyo}} I don't like it, I don't want it

blocks.p: **Me too: {{도|do}}.** {{도|do}} means “too, also”, and it **takes the place of** {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}}, {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}} or {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}: {{저도 좋아해요|jeodo joahaeyo}} “I like it too”, {{김치도 좋아해요|gimchido joahaeyo}} “I like kimchi too”. On its own: {{저도요!|jeodoyo!}} “Me too!”.

**Contrast: {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}}.** When you compare, {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}} marks each side: {{저는 커피를 좋아해요. 동생은 차를 좋아해요.|jeoneun keopireul joahaeyo. dongsaengeun chareul joahaeyo.}} “I like coffee; my younger sibling likes tea.” This is the second big job of {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}}, after marking the topic: “X, as opposed to others”. Sarah's {{삼계탕은 별로 안 좋아해요|samgyetangeun byeollo an joahaeyo}} is one too: samgyetang, unlike kimchi stew.

blocks.tip: {{싫어요|sireoyo}} is strong (“I don't like it”, “No!”). To be polite about food someone offers you, {{별로 안 좋아해요|byeollo an joahaeyo}} “I don't really like it” or simply {{괜찮아요|gwaenchanayo}} “I'm fine, thanks” is kinder.

mistakes.why: {{좋아해요|joahaeyo}} takes an object: {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}. ({{커피가 좋아요|keopiga joayo}} is right too.)
{{도|do}} takes the place of {{는|neun}}: {{저도|jeodo}}.
For other people, use {{좋아해요|joahaeyo}}: {{좋아요|joayo}} says how something feels to you.

lessons.title: Ask who, what, where, when and why
lessons.summary: Ask real questions: who's coming, what you're eating, where and when you're meeting, and why.
lessons.topic: question words {{누구|nugu}}, {{뭐|mwo}}, {{어디|eodi}}, {{언제|eonje}}, {{왜|wae}}, {{어떻게|eotteoke}}, {{무슨|museun}}, {{어느|eoneu}}; {{누가|nuga}} “who” as the subject

goal.tr: When are you going to Korea?

dialog.tr: Who's coming tomorrow?

Where are we meeting?
We're meeting in Gangnam.

blocks.p: **The question word stays where the answer goes.** English moves question words to the front (“What do you eat?”); Korean leaves them where the answer will be: {{뭐 먹어요?|mwo meogeoyo?}} “what eat?” → {{김밥 먹어요|gimbap meogeoyo}} “gimbap eat”. The verb stays last, with the same ending as an ordinary sentence.

table: {{저 사람은 누구예요?|jeo sarameun nuguyeyo?}} Who's that?
{{뭐 먹어요?|mwo meogeoyo?}} What are you eating?
{{어디에서 만나요?|eodieseo mannayo?}} Where are we meeting?
{{언제 와요?|eonje wayo?}} When are you coming?
{{왜 한국어를 배워요?|wae hangugeoreul baewoyo?}} Why are you learning Korean?
{{어떻게 가요?|eotteoke gayo?}} How do you get there?

blocks.p: **Who: {{누구|nugu}} or {{누가|nuga}}?** When “who” is the subject, the one doing something, it's {{누가|nuga}}: {{누구|nugu}} + {{가|ga}}, shortened. {{누가 와요?|nuga wayo?}} “Who's coming?”. The answer takes {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}} too: {{민지 씨가 와요|minji ssiga wayo}}. Question words, and the answers to them, are **new information**, and new information takes {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}}, not {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}}.

**What kind, which.** {{무슨|museun}} “what (kind of)” and {{어느|eoneu}} “which” go before a noun: {{무슨 음식을 좋아해요?|museun eumsigeul joahaeyo?}} “What food do you like?”, {{어느 나라 사람이에요?|eoneu nara saramieyo?}} “Which country are you from?” (which country person-are).

ex.tr: What kind of food do you like?

blocks.tip: In speech, {{뭐|mwo}} and {{어디|eodi}} usually drop their particles: {{뭐 해요?|mwo haeyo?}}, {{어디 가요?|eodi gayo?}}. {{뭐를|mworeul}} often shortens to {{뭘|mwol}}: {{뭘 먹어요?|mwol meogeoyo?}}.

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say what things are like: big, cheap, delicious, spicy, busy. In Korean, these words work like verbs.
lessons.topic: descriptive verbs; {{아주|aju}}, {{정말|jeongmal}}, {{너무|neomu}}, {{좀|jom}}; the dropped {{ㅡ}} ({{커요|keoyo}}, {{바빠요|bappayo}}) and the {{ㅂ}} that becomes {{우|u}} ({{매워요|maewoyo}})

goal.t: 이 떡볶이는 정말 맛있어요. 좀 매워요.
goal.tr: This tteokbokki is really good. It's a bit spicy.
goal.r: i tteokbokkineun jeongmal masisseoyo. jom maewoyo.

blocks.p: **Describing words are verbs.** In Korean, “expensive”, “big”, “delicious” are verbs: {{비싸다|bissada}} means “to be expensive”. So there's no {{이에요|ieyo}}: {{비싸요|bissayo}} alone is “it's expensive”. They take the same endings as action verbs: {{-아요|-ayo}}/{{-어요|-eoyo}}, {{안|an}}, the rising voice for a question.

blocks.means: a Korean verb that describes, like {{크다|keuda}} “to be big” or {{좋다|jota}} “to be good”. English uses an adjective with “is”; Korean uses one verb.

table: there's a lot, there are many

blocks.p: **What you describe** takes {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}}, or {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}} when it's your topic: {{이 가방이 비싸요|i gabangi bissayo}} “this bag is expensive”, {{서울은 커요|seoureun keoyo}} “Seoul is big”. {{맛있어요|masisseoyo}} and {{재미있어요|jaemiisseoyo}} are “taste-exists” and “fun-exists”, so their opposites use {{없어요|eopseoyo}}: {{맛없어요|madeopseoyo}} “it doesn't taste good”, {{재미없어요|jaemieopseoyo}} “it's boring”.

**Two families that change shape.** A stem ending in {{ㅡ}} drops it, and takes {{-아요|-ayo}} or {{-어요|-eoyo}} by the vowel before: {{크다|keuda}} → {{커요|keoyo}}, {{바쁘다|bappeuda}} → {{바빠요|bappayo}}. And many stems ending in {{ㅂ}} turn it into {{우|u}}: {{맵다|maepda}} → {{매워요|maewoyo}}, {{춥다|chupda}} → {{추워요|chuwoyo}}.

**How much?** {{아주|aju}} and {{정말|jeongmal}} “very, really”, {{진짜|jinjja}} “really” (casual), {{좀|jom}} “a bit”, and {{너무|neomu}} “too”, which in everyday speech often just means “so”: {{너무 맛있어요!|neomu masisseoyo!}} “It's so good!”.

blocks.tip: No “it” is needed for the weather: {{추워요|chuwoyo}} “it's cold”, {{더워요|deowoyo}} “it's hot” ({{덥다|deopda}}). And no “I”: {{배고파요|baegopayo}} “I'm hungry” ({{배고프다|baegopeuda}}, the {{ㅡ}} drops).

mistakes.why: {{비싸다|bissada}} is already a verb: no {{이에요|ieyo}}.
{{춥다|chupda}} turns its {{ㅂ}} into {{우|u}}: {{추워요|chuwoyo}}.
The {{ㅡ}} drops: {{바빠요|bappayo}}.

lessons.summary: Order two coffees, say how many people are in your family, and how old you are.

blocks.p: **Two sets of numbers.** Korean has two sets of numbers: native Korean ({{하나|hana}}, {{둘|dul}}, {{셋|set}}…) and Sino-Korean ({{일|il}}, {{이|i}}, {{삼|sam}}…, which came from Chinese: next lesson). Native numbers are for **counting** things and people, for age, and for the hours of the clock.

blocks.means: a word that comes after a number to say what kind of thing is counted, like “two **cups** of coffee” in English. Korean uses one for almost everything: {{두 잔|du jan}} “two cups”, {{세 명|se myeong}} “three people”.

blocks.p: **Number + counter.** Korean counts like “coffee two cups”: the thing, the number, then a counter: {{커피 두 잔|keopi du jan}}. The numbers 1 to 4 and 20 get shorter before a counter: {{하나|hana}} → {{한|han}}, {{둘|dul}} → {{두|du}}, {{셋|set}} → {{세|se}}, {{넷|net}} → {{네|ne}}, {{스물|seumul}} → {{스무|seumu}}. So do 11 and 12: {{열한 개|yeolhan gae}}, {{열두 개|yeoldu gae}}.

blocks.p: **How many?** {{몇|myeot}} “how many” goes before the counter: {{몇 명이에요?|myeot myeongieyo?}} “How many people?”, {{몇 살이에요?|myeot sarieyo?}} “How old are you?”. And {{하고|hago}} after a noun joins it to the next one: {{커피하고 물|keopihago mul}} “coffee and water”.

lessons.title: Ask prices and give numbers
lessons.summary: Ask how much something is, understand the answer, and give a phone number or a date.
lessons.topic: Sino-Korean numbers {{일|il}}, {{이|i}}, {{삼|sam}}…, {{백|baek}}, {{천|cheon}}, {{만|man}}; {{원|won}}; {{얼마예요?|eolmayeyo?}}; phone numbers, months and dates

dialog.tr: Excuse me, how much are these apples?
A thousand won each.
Then five, please.
Sure, that's five thousand won.
Here's ten thousand won.
Five thousand won change. Thank you!

blocks.p: **Sino-Korean numbers** came from Chinese and are used for money, phone numbers, dates, minutes and floors. They are very regular: learn 1 to 10, then build. 11 is “ten one” {{십일|sibil}}, 20 is “two ten” {{이십|isip}}, 35 is “three ten five” {{삼십오|samsibo}}.

**Big numbers.** {{백|baek}} is 100, {{천|cheon}} 1,000 and, the important one, {{만|man}} **10,000**. Korean counts big numbers in ten-thousands, not thousands: 50,000 is {{오만|oman}} “five ten-thousands”, 120,000 is {{십이만|sibiman}}. On their own, {{백|baek}}, {{천|cheon}} and {{만|man}} already mean one of them: not {{일만|ilman}}. Korean won are small: 10,000 won is about seven or eight US dollars.
**How much?** {{얼마예요?|eolmayeyo?}} is “How much is it?”. The answer is the number, {{원|won}}, and {{이에요|ieyo}}: {{삼천 원이에요|samcheon wonieyo}} “It's 3,000 won.” {{한 개에|han gaee}} is “for one, each”.

**Phone numbers and dates.** Phone numbers are said digit by digit, with {{공|gong}} for zero: 010-1234-5678 is {{공일공 일이삼사 오육칠팔|gongilgong irisamsa oyukchilpal}}. A month is a number + {{월|wol}}, a day a number + {{일|il}}: {{오월 오일|owol oil}} “May 5th”. Two months change: June is {{유월|yuwol}}, October {{시월|siwol}}.

ex.tr: I live on the third floor.
Could you give me a discount?
ex.note: word for word “please cut it down a little”

blocks.tip: In shops and markets, Koreans call the owner {{사장님|sajangnim}} “boss”: it's friendly and polite. And in a market, {{좀 깎아 주세요|jom kkakka juseyo}} sometimes works!

June is {{유월|yuwol}}: the {{ㄱ}} drops. October is {{시월|siwol}}.
{{원|won}} ends in a consonant: {{이에요|ieyo}}.

lessons.title: Say when you do things
lessons.summary: Tell the time, say what time you get up or meet, and from when until when you work.
lessons.topic: {{시|si}} (native numbers) and {{분|bun}} (Sino-Korean); {{에|e}} for time; {{부터|buteo}} … {{까지|kkaji}}; the days of the week

goal.tr: I get up at seven in the morning.

dialog.tr: What time is it now?
It's half past three.
What time is the meeting?
It's at four.

From four to five.

blocks.p: **Two kinds of numbers in one time.** Hours use native numbers ({{한 시|han si}}, {{두 시|du si}}, {{세 시|se si}}…), minutes use Sino-Korean ones ({{십 분|sip bun}}, {{삼십 분|samsip bun}}): {{세 시 이십 분|se si isip bun}} is 3:20. {{반|ban}} is “half”: {{세 시 반|se si ban}} “half past three”.

table: {{세 시 십오 분|se si sibo bun}}
{{열한 시 오 분|yeolhan si o bun}}

blocks.p: **At a time: {{에|e}}.** The same {{에|e}} as for places: {{일곱 시에 일어나요|ilgop sie ireonayo}} “I get up at seven”, {{주말에|jumare}} “at the weekend”, {{월요일에|woryoire}} “on Monday”. But {{오늘|oneul}} “today”, {{내일|naeil}} “tomorrow”, {{어제|eoje}} “yesterday” and {{지금|jigeum}} “now” don't take it: {{내일 만나요|naeil mannayo}} “see you tomorrow”.

**From… until: {{부터|buteo}} … {{까지|kkaji}}.** {{아홉 시부터 여섯 시까지 일해요|ahop sibuteo yeoseot sikkaji ilhaeyo}} “I work from nine to six”. Put {{아침|achim}} “morning”, {{오후|ohu}} “afternoon, p.m.”, {{저녁|jeonyeok}} “evening” or {{밤|bam}} “night” before the hour: {{저녁 일곱 시|jeonyeok ilgop si}} “7 in the evening”.

ex.tr: The bank is open until 4 p.m.
ex.note: {{해요|haeyo}} “does”: for a shop or a bank, “is open”

There are classes from Monday to Friday.

A time takes {{에|e}}, not {{에서|eseo}}.

lessons.title: Ask someone to do something
lessons.summary: Ask people politely to speak slowly, wait, sit down or take you somewhere, and tell them not to worry.
lessons.topic: {{-(으)세요|-(eu)seyo}} “please do”; {{-아/어 주세요|-a/eo juseyo}} “please do (for me)”; {{-지 마세요|-ji maseyo}} “please don't”; the helping vowel {{으|eu}}

dialog.tr: Hello. Where are you going?
To Myeongdong, please.
Sure. Please fasten your seat belt.
Driver, could you go a little slower, please?
Sure, don't worry.

blocks.p: **Please do: {{-(으)세요|-(eu)seyo}}.** Add {{-세요|-seyo}} to a stem ending in a vowel, {{-으세요|-euseyo}} to one ending in a consonant: {{가세요|gaseyo}} “please go”, {{앉으세요|anjeuseyo}} “please sit down”. It's the polite way to tell someone what to do: directions, instructions, invitations. {{어서 오세요|eoseo oseyo}} “welcome” is “please come quickly”.

blocks.means: the vowel {{으|eu}} that some endings add after a stem ending in a consonant, so two consonants don't meet: {{앉|an}} + {{세요|seyo}} → {{앉으세요|anjeuseyo}}. It's written {{(으)|(eu)}} in endings.

blocks.p: **Please do it for me: {{-아/어 주세요|-a/eo juseyo}}.** When you ask a favor, something done **for you**, take the present form, drop {{요|yo}}, and add {{주세요|juseyo}} “please give”: {{말해요|malhaeyo}} → {{말해 주세요|malhae juseyo}} “please say (it for me)”. This is the softer, more usual way to ask for something.
**Please don't: {{-지 마세요|-ji maseyo}}.** Stem + {{-지 마세요|-ji maseyo}}: {{가지 마세요|gaji maseyo}} “please don't go”, {{걱정하지 마세요|geokjeonghaji maseyo}} “don't worry”.

ex.tr: Could you say that again, please?
Could you open the door, please?
Could you take a picture of us, please?

blocks.tip: {{-(으)세요|-(eu)seyo}} is also the polite way to **ask** about someone: {{어디 가세요?|eodi gaseyo?}} “Where are you going?” (to someone you respect). You'll see why in lesson 29.

mistakes.why: {{앉|an}} ends in a consonant: add the helping vowel, {{-으세요|-euseyo}}.
Stems ending in {{ㄹ}} drop it before {{-세요|-seyo}}: {{만드세요|mandeuseyo}}.
{{주세요|juseyo}} goes after the present form without {{요|yo}}: {{말해|malhae}}, not the stem.

blocks.p: **The past comes from the present.** Take the present form without {{요|yo}}, tuck {{ㅆ}} under its last syllable, and add {{어요|eoyo}}: {{가(요)|ga(yo)}} → {{갔어요|gasseoyo}} “I went”, {{먹어(요)|meogeo(yo)}} → {{먹었어요|meogeosseoyo}} “I ate”, {{해(요)|hae(yo)}} → {{했어요|haesseoyo}} “I did”. So the past follows the same vowel harmony as the present: {{-았어요|-asseoyo}} after {{ㅏ}} and {{ㅗ}}, {{-었어요|-eosseoyo}} after other vowels, {{했어요|haesseoyo}} for {{하다|hada}}.

**One past for many.** Korean's everyday past covers several English tenses: {{먹었어요|meogeosseoyo}} is “I ate” and “I've eaten”. As in the present, the same form works for “I”, “you” and “she”: {{뭐 했어요?|mwo haesseoyo?}} “What did you do?”.

**Not: {{안|an}} + the past.** {{안 갔어요|an gasseoyo}} “I didn't go”, {{공부 안 했어요|gongbu an haesseoyo}} “I didn't study”. {{아무것도 안 했어요|amugeotdo an haesseoyo}} is “I didn't do anything”. Words for the past: {{어제|eoje}} “yesterday”, {{지난주|jinanju}} “last week”, {{지난 주말|jinan jumal}} “last weekend”, {{작년|jangnyeon}} “last year”, {{아까|akka}} “a moment ago”.

ex.tr: I went to Busan last week.

blocks.tip: Two common verbs change shape before a vowel. {{듣다|deutda}} “to listen” turns its {{ㄷ}} into {{ㄹ}}: {{들어요|deureoyo}}, {{들었어요|deureosseoyo}} (so does {{걷다|geotda}} “to walk”: {{걸어요|georeoyo}}). {{모르다|moreuda}} “not to know” doubles its {{ㄹ}}: {{몰라요|mollayo}}, {{몰랐어요|mollasseoyo}}.

lessons.title: Say how it was
lessons.summary: Say how your weekend, the food or your trip was, and what someone used to be: “The trip was really fun.”
lessons.topic: the past of descriptive verbs ({{좋았어요|joasseoyo}}, {{추웠어요|chuwosseoyo}}, {{바빴어요|bappasseoyo}}); {{이었어요|ieosseoyo}} / {{였어요|yeosseoyo}}; {{어땠어요?|eottaesseoyo?}}

dialog.tr: How was your trip to Jeju?
It was great! The sea was so beautiful.
And the weather?
It was a bit cold. But it was still fun.
How was the food?
The black pork was really delicious.

blocks.p: **Describing in the past.** Descriptive verbs take the same past ending as action verbs: {{좋아요|joayo}} → {{좋았어요|joasseoyo}} “it was good”, {{재미있어요|jaemiisseoyo}} → {{재미있었어요|jaemiisseosseoyo}} “it was fun”. The families that change shape (lesson 12) keep their present shape: {{추워요|chuwoyo}} → {{추웠어요|chuwosseoyo}}, {{바빠요|bappayo}} → {{바빴어요|bappasseoyo}}, {{예뻐요|yeppeoyo}} → {{예뻤어요|yeppeosseoyo}}.

**Was a…: {{이었어요|ieosseoyo}}/{{였어요|yeosseoyo}}.** The past of {{이에요|ieyo}}/{{예요|yeyo}} is {{이었어요|ieosseoyo}} after a consonant and {{였어요|yeosseoyo}} after a vowel: {{학생이었어요|haksaengieosseoyo}} “I was a student”, {{의사였어요|uisayeosseoyo}} “she was a doctor”. And {{아니에요|anieyo}} becomes {{아니었어요|anieosseoyo}} “it wasn't”.

**How was it?** {{어땠어요?|eottaesseoyo?}}, the past of {{어때요?|eottaeyo?}} “how is it?”, asks for a description: {{영화 어땠어요?|yeonghwa eottaesseoyo?}} “How was the movie?”. In questions like this, the topic often drops its particle.

ex.tr: I was a student last year.

blocks.tip: {{그래도|geuraedo}} “still, even so” is handy after something negative: {{좀 추웠어요. 그래도 재미있었어요.|jom chuwosseoyo. geuraedo jaemiisseosseoyo.}} “It was a bit cold. But it was still fun.”

lessons.title: Say one thing, then another
lessons.summary: Join two actions or two descriptions into one sentence: “I had breakfast and went to work”, “It's cheap and good.”
lessons.topic: stem + {{-고|-go}} “and, and then”; the tense on the last verb; {{그리고|geurigo}}

goal.tr: I had breakfast and went to work.

dialog.tr: What did you do yesterday evening?

blocks.p: **And, and then: {{-고|-go}}.** Stem + {{-고|-go}} joins two sentences into one: {{아침을 먹어요. 회사에 가요.|achimeul meogeoyo. hoesae gayo.}} → {{아침을 먹고 회사에 가요.|achimeul meokgo hoesae gayo.}} “I have breakfast and go to work.” You know this {{-고|-go}} from {{-고 싶어요|-go sipeoyo}}: it goes straight onto the stem and never changes shape.

**The last verb says when.** In a chain of actions, the {{-고|-go}} verb usually has no past ending: the last verb says when everything happened. {{아침을 먹고 회사에 갔어요|achimeul meokgo hoesae gasseoyo}} is “I had breakfast and went to work”.

table: {{밥을 먹고 커피를 마셔요.|babeul meokgo keopireul masyeoyo.}}
I eat and then drink coffee.
{{밥을 먹고 커피를 마셨어요.|babeul meokgo keopireul masyeosseoyo.}}
I ate and then drank coffee.

blocks.p: **Two descriptions** join the same way: {{이 방은 넓고 깨끗해요|i bangeun neolgo kkaekkeutaeyo}} “This room is big and clean.” With {{이에요|ieyo}}, it's {{이고|igo}}: {{동생은 학생이고 저는 회사원이에요|dongsaengeun haksaengigo jeoneun hoesawonieyo}} “My younger sibling is a student, and I'm an office worker.” Between two separate sentences, {{그리고|geurigo}} “and, and also” does the same job: {{밥을 먹었어요. 그리고 커피를 마셨어요.|babeul meogeosseoyo. geurigo keopireul masyeosseoyo.}}

ex.tr: I shower and then have breakfast.
I did my homework and went to bed.
This restaurant is cheap and good.
My younger sibling is tall and funny.
ex.note: {{키가 크다|kiga keuda}} “to be tall”: height is big

blocks.tip: Korean likes long chains: {{일어나고, 샤워하고, 아침을 먹고, 회사에 가요.|ireonago, syawohago, achimeul meokgo, hoesae gayo.}} Only the last verb has the full ending.

mistakes.why: {{-고|-go}} goes straight onto the stem: {{먹고|meokgo}}.

mistakes.tr: I'm a student, and my younger sibling is an office worker.
mistakes.why: After a consonant, {{이에요|ieyo}} joins as {{이고|igo}}.

lessons.title: Say who you were with and how you went
lessons.summary: Say who you did things with, and how you got there: by bus, by subway, on foot.
lessons.topic: {{하고|hago}}, {{(이)랑|(i)rang}}, {{와|wa}}/{{과|gwa}} “with, and”; {{같이|gachi}}, {{혼자|honja}}; {{(으)로|(eu)ro}} “by, with, in”

goal.tr: I went by subway with a friend.

dialog.tr: Who did you have dinner with yesterday?

In Sinchon. I went by bus.

dialog.t: 저는 혼자 먹었어요. 다음에는 같이 가요!

blocks.p: **With someone: {{하고|hago}}.** The {{하고|hago}} that joins nouns ({{커피하고 물|keopihago mul}}, lesson 13) also means “with”: {{친구하고 먹었어요|chinguhago meogeosseoyo}} “I ate with a friend”. {{같이|gachi}} “together” often follows: {{친구하고 같이 갔어요|chinguhago gachi gasseoyo}}. And {{혼자|honja}} is “alone”, with no particle.
**Three words for “and, with”.** They mean the same and differ in style. {{이랑|irang}} and {{과|gwa}} come after a consonant, {{랑|rang}} and {{와|wa}} after a vowel.

**By, with, in: {{(으)로|(eu)ro}}.** After a means of transport, a tool or a language, {{(으)로|(eu)ro}} says how: {{버스로|beoseuro}} “by bus”, {{손으로|soneuro}} “by hand”, {{한국어로|hangugeoro}} “in Korean”. It's {{으로|euro}} after a consonant and {{로|ro}} after a vowel, but also {{로|ro}} after {{ㄹ}}: {{지하철로|jihacheollo}}, not {{지하철으로|jihacheoreuro}}. On foot is {{걸어서|georeoseo}} “walking”: {{걸어서 가요|georeoseo gayo}} “I walk there”.

ex.tr: I went shopping with a friend.
I go to work by subway every day.
I went to the beach with my family at the weekend.
In Korea, people eat rice with a spoon.
ex.note: chopsticks are for the side dishes

blocks.tip: {{(이)랑|(i)rang}} is what you'll hear most among friends; {{와|wa}}/{{과|gwa}} is what you'll read. When unsure, {{하고|hago}} always fits.

mistakes.why: After {{ㄹ}}, just {{로|ro}}.
How you go: {{(으)로|(eu)ro}}. ({{버스에서|beoseueseo}} is “on the bus”, where something happens.)
“With someone” is {{하고|hago}} (or {{랑|rang}}, {{와|wa}}/{{과|gwa}}), not the object particle.

lessons.title: Say what you're going to do
lessons.summary: Talk about your plans for tomorrow, the weekend or next year, and make guesses: “It'll probably rain.”
lessons.topic: {{-(으)ㄹ 거예요|-(eu)l geoyeyo}} “will, going to”; {{내일|naeil}}, {{다음 주|daeum ju}}, {{이번 주말|ibeon jumal}}; {{아마|ama}} “probably”

blocks.p: **Will, going to: {{-(으)ㄹ 거예요|-(eu)l geoyeyo}}.** Add {{-ㄹ 거예요|-l geoyeyo}} to a stem ending in a vowel, {{-을 거예요|-eul geoyeyo}} to one ending in a consonant: {{갈 거예요|gal geoyeyo}} “I'm going to go”, {{먹을 거예요|meogeul geoyeyo}} “I'm going to eat”. Stems ending in {{ㄹ}} just add {{거예요|geoyeyo}}: {{살 거예요|sal geoyeyo}}, {{만들 거예요|mandeul geoyeyo}}. It's the everyday way to talk about plans and the future. {{거|geo}} is “thing”: word for word, “it's a thing I'll go”.

**Guesses.** The same ending makes a guess about something you can't know for sure: {{내일은 추울 거예요|naeireun chuul geoyeyo}} “It'll be cold tomorrow.” With {{아마|ama}} “probably”: {{아마 비가 올 거예요|ama biga ol geoyeyo}} “It'll probably rain.”

**Not going to, and questions.** {{안|an}} goes before the verb as always: {{안 갈 거예요|an gal geoyeyo}} “I'm not going to go”. And {{뭐 할 거예요?|mwo hal geoyeyo?}} “What are you going to do?”. Future words: {{내일|naeil}} “tomorrow”, {{모레|more}} “the day after tomorrow”, {{이번 주말|ibeon jumal}} “this weekend”, {{다음 주|daeum ju}} “next week”, {{다음 달|daeum dal}} “next month”, {{내년|naenyeon}} “next year”, {{나중에|najunge}} “later”.

ex.tr: What are you going to do tomorrow?
I'm going to move next month.

lessons.title: Suggest doing something together
lessons.summary: Invite someone, suggest a time and a place, offer to help, and say yes or no politely: “Shall we have lunch together?”
lessons.topic: {{-(으)ㄹ까요?|-(eu)lkkayo?}} “shall we?, shall I?”; {{-아/어요|-a/eoyo}} for “let's”; N + {{어때요?|eottaeyo?}} “how about…?”; {{-(으)ㅂ시다|-(eu)psida}} to recognise

dialog.t: 내일 시간 있어요? 같이 영화 볼까요?
dialog.tr: Are you free tomorrow? Shall we see a movie?
dialog.r: naeil sigan isseoyo? gachi yeonghwa bolkkayo?

dialog.tr: Sure! What time shall we meet?
How about six?
Good. Where shall we meet?
Let's meet in front of the cinema.
Okay, see you tomorrow then!

blocks.p: **Shall we? {{-(으)ㄹ까요?|-(eu)lkkayo?}}** Stem + {{-ㄹ까요?|-lkkayo?}} after a vowel, {{-을까요?|-eulkkayo?}} after a consonant: {{같이 갈까요?|gachi galkkayo?}} “Shall we go together?”, {{뭐 먹을까요?|mwo meogeulkkayo?}} “What shall we eat?”. It's the same {{ㄹ}} as in {{-(으)ㄹ 거예요|-(eu)l geoyeyo}}, with the same {{ㄹ}} stems: {{놀까요?|nolkkayo?}}

**Shall I?** With {{제가|jega}} “I” ({{저|jeo}} + {{가|ga}}), the same ending offers to do something: {{제가 할까요?|jega halkkayo?}} “Shall I do it?”, {{창문을 열까요?|changmuneul yeolkkayo?}} “Shall I open the window?”.

**Let's, and how about.** The ordinary present can also mean “let's”, from the situation and your tone: {{같이 가요!|gachi gayo!}} “Let's go together!”, {{내일 봐요!|naeil bwayo!}} “See you tomorrow!”. And a noun + {{어때요?|eottaeyo?}} is “how about…?”: {{여섯 시 어때요?|yeoseot si eottaeyo?}} “How about six?”. {{-(으)ㅂ시다|-(eu)psida}} ({{갑시다|gapsida}} “let's go”) is a formal “let's” from a leader to a group; don't say it to someone older than you.

**Saying yes or no.** Yes: {{좋아요!|joayo!}} “Great!”, {{그래요.|geuraeyo.}} “Okay.” No, politely: {{미안해요, 다음에 같이 가요.|mianhaeyo, daeume gachi gayo.}} “Sorry, let's go together another time.” Koreans often soften a no by leaving it unfinished: {{그날은 좀…|geunareun jom…}} “That day is a bit…”.

ex.tr: Shall we go hiking at the weekend?
Let's just rest at home today.

ex.note: formal: a leader to a group

blocks.tip: {{-(으)ㄹ까요?|-(eu)lkkayo?}} also asks for advice: {{뭐 입을까요?|mwo ibeulkkayo?}} “What should I wear?”, {{어떻게 할까요?|eotteoke halkkayo?}} “What should we do?”.

mistakes.why: {{먹|meok}} ends in a consonant: {{-을까요|-eulkkayo}}.
Stems ending in {{ㄹ}} just take {{-까요|-kkayo}}.
{{-(으)ㅂ시다|-(eu)psida}} is a leader's “let's” and sounds bossy to someone older; {{-(으)세요|-(eu)seyo}} is polite.

lessons.title: Say what you can and can't do
lessons.summary: Say what you can do, what you can't, and what you know how to do: “I can speak a little Korean.”
lessons.topic: {{-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요|-(eu)l su isseoyo}} / {{없어요|eopseoyo}} “can, can't”; {{못|mot}} + verb; {{-(으)ㄹ 줄 알아요|-(eu)l jul arayo}} / {{몰라요|mollayo}} “know how to”

I can go on Sunday!

blocks.p: **Can: {{-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요|-(eu)l su isseoyo}}.** Stem + {{-ㄹ 수 있어요|-l su isseoyo}} after a vowel, {{-을 수 있어요|-eul su isseoyo}} after a consonant, word for word “there is a way to…”: {{갈 수 있어요|gal su isseoyo}} “I can go”, {{먹을 수 있어요|meogeul su isseoyo}} “I can eat”. For “can't”, {{없어요|eopseoyo}} takes the place of {{있어요|isseoyo}}: {{갈 수 없어요|gal su eopseoyo}}. Stems ending in {{ㄹ}}: {{만들 수 있어요|mandeul su isseoyo}}.

**Can't, the short way: {{못|mot}}.** As {{안|an}} means “not”, {{못|mot}} before a verb means “can't”: {{못 가요|mot gayo}} “I can't go”, {{못 먹어요|mot meogeoyo}} “I can't eat it”. With a noun + {{하다|hada}} verb it goes in between: {{운동 못 해요|undong mot haeyo}}. In conversation {{못|mot}} is more common than {{-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요|-(eu)l su eopseoyo}}. With the past, it's “couldn't”: {{못 잤어요|mot jasseoyo}} “I couldn't sleep”.

table: {{안 먹어요|an meogeoyo}} I don't eat it
{{못 먹어요|mot meogeoyo}} I can't eat it
{{수영 안 해요|suyeong an haeyo}} I don't swim
{{수영 못 해요|suyeong mot haeyo}} I can't swim

blocks.p: **Know how to: {{-(으)ㄹ 줄 알아요|-(eu)l jul arayo}}.** For skills, Koreans often say “I know how to”: {{운전할 줄 알아요|unjeonhal jul arayo}} “I can drive”, {{한글을 읽을 줄 알아요|hangeureul ilgeul jul arayo}} “I can read Hangul”. And {{몰라요|mollayo}} for “don't know how”: {{수영할 줄 몰라요|suyeonghal jul mollayo}} “I can't swim”.

ex.tr: I don't know how to drive.

blocks.p: **Have to: {{-아/어야 해요|-a/eoya haeyo}}.** Take the present form without {{요|yo}} and add {{야 해요|ya haeyo}}: {{가요|gayo}} → {{가야 해요|gaya haeyo}} “I have to go”, {{먹어요|meogeoyo}} → {{먹어야 해요|meogeoya haeyo}}, {{해요|haeyo}} → {{해야 해요|haeya haeyo}}. {{-아/어야 돼요|-a/eoya dwaeyo}} means the same and is just as common in speech.

**May I? {{-아/어도 돼요?|-a/eodo dwaeyo?}}** The present form without {{요|yo}}, then {{도 돼요|do dwaeyo}}, word for word “even if I do, it's fine?”: {{앉아도 돼요?|anjado dwaeyo?}} “May I sit down?”, {{들어가도 돼요?|deureogado dwaeyo?}} “May I come in?”. The answer: {{네, 돼요|ne, dwaeyo}} or {{네, 앉아도 돼요|ne, anjado dwaeyo}}.

**Must not: {{-(으)면 안 돼요|-(eu)myeon an dwaeyo}}.** Stem + {{-면 안 돼요|-myeon an dwaeyo}} after a vowel, {{-으면 안 돼요|-eumyeon an dwaeyo}} after a consonant, word for word “if you do it, it won't do”: {{여기에서 담배를 피우면 안 돼요|yeogieseo dambaereul piumyeon an dwaeyo}} “You can't smoke here.” ({{-(으)면|-(eu)myeon}} “if” has a lesson of its own: lesson 27.) And **don't have to** is “it's fine even if you don't”: {{안 가도 돼요|an gado dwaeyo}} “You don't have to go.”

blocks.p: **In the middle of it: {{-고 있어요|-go isseoyo}}.** Stem + {{-고 있어요|-go isseoyo}}, word for word “am in doing”: {{먹고 있어요|meokgo isseoyo}} “I'm eating”, {{기다리고 있어요|gidarigo isseoyo}} “I'm waiting”. It's the {{-고|-go}} of lesson 19 with {{있어요|isseoyo}} “am (there)”.

**When do you need it?** Less often than in English: the plain present {{뭐 해요?|mwo haeyo?}} already means “What are you doing?”. Use {{-고 있어요|-go isseoyo}} to stress that something is going on **right now**, or **these days**: {{요즘 한국어를 배우고 있어요|yojeum hangugeoreul baeugo isseoyo}} “I'm learning Korean these days.” In the past, {{-고 있었어요|-go isseosseoyo}} is “I was …-ing”.

lessons.title: Talk about plans you've made
lessons.summary: Say what you're planning to do, what you've decided, and why: “I'm planning to learn to cook.”
lessons.topic: {{-(으)려고 해요|-(eu)ryeogo haeyo}} “I'm planning to”; {{-기로 했어요|-giro haesseoyo}} “I've decided to, we've agreed to”; {{-(으)려고|-(eu)ryeogo}} “in order to”

goal.tr: I'm planning to work in Korea next year.

blocks.p: **Planning to: {{-(으)려고 해요|-(eu)ryeogo haeyo}}.** Stem + {{-려고 해요|-ryeogo haeyo}} after a vowel or {{ㄹ}}, {{-으려고 해요|-euryeogo haeyo}} after another consonant: {{배우려고 해요|baeuryeogo haeyo}}, {{만들려고 해요|mandeullyeogo haeyo}}, {{먹으려고 해요|meogeuryeogo haeyo}}. It means “I intend to, I'm thinking of”: softer than {{-(으)ㄹ 거예요|-(eu)l geoyeyo}}, a plan that isn't settled yet.

**Decided: {{-기로 했어요|-giro haesseoyo}}.** Stem + {{-기로 했어요|-giro haesseoyo}}, “(I) decided to, (we) agreed to”: {{가기로 했어요|gagiro haesseoyo}}. It's how Koreans talk about arrangements: {{토요일에 만나기로 했어요|toyoire mannagiro haesseoyo}} “We're meeting on Saturday” (we agreed).

table: I've decided to travel. / We've agreed to.

blocks.p: **In order to: {{-(으)려고|-(eu)ryeogo}}.** Without {{해요|haeyo}}, {{-(으)려고|-(eu)ryeogo}} gives a purpose: {{한국 친구를 사귀려고 한국어를 배워요|hanguk chingureul sagwiryeogo hangugeoreul baewoyo}} “I'm learning Korean to make Korean friends.”

blocks.tip: With {{-(으)려고 했어요|-(eu)ryeogo haesseoyo}} (past), you planned to but didn't: {{어제 운동하려고 했어요. 그런데 너무 피곤했어요.|eoje undongharyeogo haesseoyo. geureonde neomu pigonhaesseoyo.}} “I meant to work out yesterday. But I was too tired.”

lessons.title: Say what happens if…
lessons.summary: Talk about conditions: “If it rains, let's stay in”, “When you get home, text me”, “All you have to do is press this.”
lessons.topic: {{-(으)면|-(eu)myeon}} “if, when”; {{-(으)면 돼요|-(eu)myeon dwaeyo}} “all you need to do is”

goal.tr: If you have time, let's watch a movie together.

dialog.tr: What shall we do if it rains tomorrow?
If it rains, let's watch a movie at home.
Okay. And if the weather's nice?
If it's nice, let's go to the Han River park!
Then I'll text you when I get up tomorrow morning.

blocks.p: **If: {{-(으)면|-(eu)myeon}}.** Stem + {{-면|-myeon}} after a vowel or {{ㄹ}}, {{-으면|-eumyeon}} after another consonant: {{비가 오면|biga omyeon}} “if it rains”, {{길을 알면|gireul almyeon}} “if you know the way”, {{시간이 있으면|sigani isseumyeon}} “if you have time”. The {{-(으)면|-(eu)myeon}} part comes first, then what happens: {{비가 오면 집에 있을 거예요|biga omyeon jibe isseul geoyeyo}} “If it rains, I'll stay at home.”

**If and when.** {{-(으)면|-(eu)myeon}} is also “when, whenever” for something that will surely happen: {{집에 도착하면 문자 주세요|jibe dochakamyeon munja juseyo}} “When you get home, text me.”, {{봄이 오면|bomi omyeon}} “when spring comes”. As with {{-고|-go}}, the {{-(으)면|-(eu)myeon}} verb has no tense of its own: the last verb says when.

**All you need to do: {{-(으)면 돼요|-(eu)myeon dwaeyo}}.** Word for word “if you do it, it works”: {{여기에 이름을 쓰면 돼요|yeogie ireumeul sseumyeon dwaeyo}} “You just need to write your name here.” As a question, it asks what to do: {{어떻게 하면 돼요?|eotteoke hamyeon dwaeyo?}} “What do I need to do?”. Its opposite is {{-(으)면 안 돼요|-(eu)myeon an dwaeyo}} “mustn't” from lesson 24.

ex.tr: If you're tired, have a rest.

lessons.summary: Ask how to get somewhere, follow directions, take the subway, and say how long it takes.
lessons.topic: {{에서|eseo}} … {{까지|kkaji}} “from… to”; {{(으)로|(eu)ro}} “towards”; {{걸려요|geollyeoyo}} “it takes (time)”; {{돌다|dolda}} → {{도세요|doseyo}}

goal.tr: How do I get from here to Myeongdong?

blocks.p: **From… to: {{에서|eseo}} … {{까지|kkaji}}.** For places, “from” is {{에서|eseo}} (lesson 8) and “to, as far as” is {{까지|kkaji}}: {{집에서 회사까지|jibeseo hoesakkaji}} “from home to work”. For times it's {{부터|buteo}} … {{까지|kkaji}} (lesson 15).

**Towards: {{(으)로|(eu)ro}}.** The {{(으)로|(eu)ro}} of “by bus” also means “towards”: {{오른쪽으로 가세요|oreunjjogeuro gaseyo}} “go right”, {{이쪽으로 오세요|ijjogeuro oseyo}} “come this way”, {{명동으로 가 주세요|myeongdongeuro ga juseyo}} “to Myeongdong, please”. With {{가다|gada}} and {{오다|oda}}, {{에|e}} names the place you arrive at, {{(으)로|(eu)ro}} the direction you head in; often both work.

table: Get off at the next station.
Change trains at City Hall Station.

blocks.p: **Getting on and off.** You get on something with {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}} ({{버스를 타요|beoseureul tayo}}) and off it with {{에서|eseo}} ({{버스에서 내려요|beoseueseo naeryeoyo}}). {{돌다|dolda}} “to turn” is an {{ㄹ}} verb: {{도세요|doseyo}} “please turn”.

**How long does it take? {{얼마나 걸려요?|eolmana geollyeoyo?}}** {{걸려요|geollyeoyo}} (from {{걸리다|geollida}}) is “it takes (time)”: {{버스로 삼십 분 걸려요|beoseuro samsip bun geollyeoyo}} “It takes thirty minutes by bus.” {{쯤|jjeum}} after a number is “about”: {{십 분쯤|sip bunjjeum}} “about ten minutes”.

ex.tr: Excuse me, where's the subway station?

Change to Line 2 at City Hall Station.

blocks.tip: {{실례합니다|sillyehamnida}} “excuse me” (word for word “I'm being rude”) is the polite way to stop a stranger. {{저기요|jeogiyo}} works too.

mistakes.why: {{돌다|dolda}} is an {{ㄹ}} verb: the {{ㄹ}} drops before {{-세요|-seyo}}.
{{걸려요|geollyeoyo}} is “it takes (time)”; {{걸어요|georeoyo}} is “I walk”.
You get off **from** something: {{에서 내리다|eseo naerida}}. You get on with {{을|eul}}/{{를|reul}}: {{지하철을 타세요|jihacheoreul taseyo}}.

lessons.title: Talk politely about older people
lessons.summary: Talk about your grandparents, your boss or your teacher with respect, and ask them questions politely.

blocks.p: **Respect inside the verb.** Korean shows respect for the **person you're talking about** (or to) inside the verb, with {{-(으)시-|-(eu)si-}}. In the present, it's stem + {{-세요|-seyo}} or {{-으세요|-euseyo}}: the same form as “please do” in lesson 16. {{할머니가 텔레비전을 보세요|halmeoniga tellebijeoneul boseyo}} “Grandma is watching TV.” Use it for older people, your boss, teachers, customers and strangers older than you, but **never for yourself**.

blocks.means: a form that shows respect for the person you're talking about. In Korean: {{-(으)시-|-(eu)si-}} in the verb, and special respectful words like {{드시다|deusida}} “to eat”.

blocks.p: **Special verbs.** A few everyday verbs have their own respectful word instead of {{-시-|-si-}}. Note the two kinds of {{있다|itda}}: “to have” is {{있으세요|isseuseyo}} ({{시간 있으세요?|sigan isseuseyo?}}), “to be somewhere” is {{계세요|gyeseyo}}.

**Respectful nouns and particles.** {{님|nim}} after a title adds respect: {{선생님|seonsaengnim}} “teacher”, {{사장님|sajangnim}} “boss”, {{부장님|bujangnim}} “department head”, {{기사님|gisanim}} “driver”. In formal speech the subject particle becomes {{께서|kkeseo}}: {{할아버지께서 오셨어요|harabeojikkeseo osyeosseoyo}}. In everyday talk, {{이|i}}/{{가|ga}} or {{은|eun}}/{{는|neun}} with {{-시-|-si-}} is enough.

ex.tr: My father works at a bank.
The boss isn't here right now.

ex.note: {{진지|jinji}} is the respectful word for “a meal”

ex.tr: Do you have a moment, sir?

blocks.tip: {{-(으)세요|-(eu)seyo}} now has two jobs you know: “please do” ({{앉으세요|anjeuseyo}} “please sit”) and “you/they do, with respect” ({{어디 가세요?|eodi gaseyo?}} “where are you going?”). Your tone and the situation tell them apart.

lessons.title: Understand announcements and formal speech
lessons.summary: Understand the subway, the weather forecast and a shop's welcome, and use the formal style in the phrases everyone uses.
lessons.topic: the formal style {{-(스)ㅂ니다|-(seu)mnida}}, {{-(스)ㅂ니까?|-(seu)mnikka?}}, {{입니다|imnida}}; {{-(으)십시오|-(eu)sipsio}}; {{감사합니다|gamsahamnida}}, {{죄송합니다|joesonghamnida}}

blocks.p: **The formal style.** Besides the polite {{-아요|-ayo}}/{{-어요|-eoyo}} you've learned, Korean has a more formal polite style: {{-(스)ㅂ니다|-(seu)mnida}}. It's the style of announcements, the news, speeches, presentations, job interviews and staff talking to customers. It sounds official rather than warm. You need it mostly to understand, and for a handful of phrases everyone says.

**How it's built.** Stem + {{-ㅂ니다|-mnida}} after a vowel, {{-습니다|-seumnida}} after a consonant; questions end in {{-ㅂ니까?|-mnikka?}} / {{-습니까?|-seumnikka?}}. {{이에요|ieyo}} becomes {{입니다|imnida}}. Stems ending in {{ㄹ}} drop it: {{살다|salda}} → {{삽니다|samnida}}.

**Formal requests: {{-(으)십시오|-(eu)sipsio}}.** The formal “please do”: {{들어오십시오|deureoosipsio}} “please come in”, {{내리십시오|naerisipsio}} “please get off”. **The phrases everyone uses** are almost always formal: {{감사합니다|gamsahamnida}} “thank you”, {{죄송합니다|joesonghamnida}} “I'm sorry”, {{알겠습니다|algetseumnida}} “understood, certainly”, {{처음 뵙겠습니다|cheoeum boepgetseumnida}} “how do you do”, {{잘 먹겠습니다|jal meokgetseumnida}} “thank you for the meal” (before eating) and {{잘 먹었습니다|jal meogeotseumnida}} (after).

ex.tr: How do you do? I'm Michael.

ex.note: said before eating, to whoever cooked or is paying

ex.tr: The weather will be clear today.

blocks.tip: Use the formal style when you introduce yourself to a group, at an interview, or when you speak in public. With people you talk to every day, even politely, {{-아요|-ayo}}/{{-어요|-eoyo}} is warmer.

mistakes.why: {{-(스)ㅂ니다|-(seu)mnida}} already ends the sentence: no {{요|yo}}.
Stems ending in {{ㄹ}} drop it and take {{-ㅂ니다|-mnida}}: {{삽니다|samnida}}.

lessons.title: Offer help and make promises
lessons.summary: Say “I'll do it”, offer to do something for someone, and ask for a favor very politely.
lessons.topic: {{-(으)ㄹ게요|-(eu)lgeyo}} “I'll (do it)”; {{-아/어 드릴까요?|-a/eo deurilkkayo?}} / {{드릴게요|deurilgeyo}} “shall I… for you?”; {{-아/어 주시겠어요?|-a/eo jusigesseoyo?}} “would you…?”

goal.tr: I'll take a picture for you.

blocks.p: **I'll do it: {{-(으)ㄹ게요|-(eu)lgeyo}}.** Stem + {{-ㄹ게요|-lgeyo}} after a vowel, {{-을게요|-eulgeyo}} after a consonant ({{ㄹ}} stems: {{만들게요|mandeulgeyo}}). It's a promise or a decision you make right now, with the other person in mind: {{제가 할게요|jega halgeyo}} “I'll do it”, {{내일 전화할게요|naeil jeonhwahalgeyo}} “I'll call you tomorrow”, {{먼저 갈게요|meonjeo galgeyo}} “I'll head off now”. It's only for yourself, and never a question.

**{{-(으)ㄹ게요|-(eu)lgeyo}} or {{-(으)ㄹ 거예요|-(eu)l geoyeyo}}?** {{거예요|geoyeyo}} tells your plan as a fact; {{게요|geyo}} answers the other person and promises. “Who'll bring the drinks?” → {{제가 가져갈게요|jega gajyeogalgeyo}} “I'll bring them.”

table: I'm going to call tomorrow (that's my plan).
I'll call you tomorrow (you can count on it).

blocks.p: **Doing something for someone you respect: {{-아/어 드리다|-a/eo deurida}}.** {{드리다|deurida}} is the respectful {{주다|juda}} “to give”. Where you ask a favor with {{-아/어 주세요|-a/eo juseyo}}, you offer one with {{-아/어 드릴까요?|-a/eo deurilkkayo?}} “shall I… for you?” or {{-아/어 드릴게요|-a/eo deurilgeyo}} “I'll… for you”. And to ask a favor very politely: {{-아/어 주시겠어요?|-a/eo jusigesseoyo?}} “would you…, please?”, which is {{주세요|juseyo}} with {{-시-|-si-}} and the softness of a question.

table: {{문 좀 열어 주세요.|mun jom yeoreo juseyo.}}
{{문 좀 열어 주시겠어요?|mun jom yeoreo jusigesseoyo?}}
Would you open the door, please?
Shall I open the door for you?
I'll open the door for you.

ex.tr: Would you write your name here, please?

blocks.tip: {{아니에요|anieyo}} “it isn't (so)” is also the usual reply to thanks, like “not at all”, and to compliments, like “oh, no”.

mistakes.why: {{-(으)ㄹ게요|-(eu)lgeyo}} is a promise, never a question. To offer, ask with {{-(으)ㄹ까요?|-(eu)lkkayo?}}.
{{-(으)ㄹ게요|-(eu)lgeyo}} promises what **you** will do. For someone else, {{-(으)ㄹ 거예요|-(eu)l geoyeyo}}.
